newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters, UPS to resume negotiations Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters, UPS to resume negotiations Thursday.

text.p: The Teamsters union and United Parcel Service agreed on Wednesday to resume negotiations to settle a national strike that has crippled the world's largest parcel delivery company.
Union and management officials were expected to meet with federal mediators on Thursday in Washington. No specific time had been set for the talks to begin.
UPS said chief company negotiator Dave Murray was flying back to Washington from Atlanta on Wednesday evening to represent the company at the talks.
Labour Secretary Alexis Herman spoke with UPS Chairman James Kelly and Teamsters President Ron Carey on Wednesday and said she was "encouraged" the two sides had agreed to meet.
"The President and I feel strongly that both the company and the workers, as well as the American people, have much to gain in a quick resolution to this dispute," Herman said in a statement.
But Carey said he was sceptical that new negotiations would settle the strike, which entered its third day on Wednesday.
"We have seen no sign that the company has changed its attitude, so we are not particularly optimistic about these new talks," Carey said in a statement.
The last bargaining session collapsed on Sunday night with union leaders and management deadlocked in a dispute over pay, benefits and job security.
The Teamsters, which represent 185,000 UPS workers or nearly two-thirds of the company's U.S. work force, went on strike shortly after midnight EDT on Monday.

Since then, UPS has been handling less than 10 percent of its normal shipments. The strike has meant higher shipping costs and logistical nightmares for businesses, manufacturers and consumers who rely on the company to move their packages, parcels and documents.

On Wednesday, a group of chief executives from Sears, Roebuck & Co., Kmart Corp. and other big retailers called on U.S. President Bill Clinton to intervene in the work stoppage, warning that a prolonged strike could hurt economic growth.

"The economy, which is enjoying unprecedented sustained growth, could experience a sudden downward spiral if this strike continues for an extended period," said a letter to Clinton signed by 36 senior industry executives.
In a separate statement, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce warned of "irreparable harm and massive layoffs" for small- and mid-size firms if striking Teamsters were not ordered back to work at UPS.

But Clinton told a White House news conference he could only intervene in the job action by invoking the rarely used Taft-Hartley Law, which authorises the nation's chief executive to halt strikes that threaten health and safety.
"There has to be a severe damage to the country. The test is ... very high before the president can intervene," he said.

Meanwhile, thousands of Teamsters, including drivers, package sorters and loaders, continued to staff picket lines from Maine to California on Wednesday. They had backing from 2,000 unionized UPS pilots who have refused to cross Teamster picket lines.

The Teamsters blamed the strike on a company refusal to end sub-contracting and create thousands of new full-time jobs each year from part-time jobs, which account for 60 percent of the Atlanta-based company's 301,000 domestic workers.

UPS called those issues "a smoke screen," saying the real issue was the Teamsters' refusal to let the company withdraw from a multi-employer pension plan that includes 30 other companies, mostly trucking firms.
UPS controls 80 percent of the U.S. parcel delivery business, normally handling 12 million packages a day. Its daily volume equals 6 percent of gross domestic product.

The National Retail Federation, a Washington-based industry trade group, sought to illustrate the strike's potential impact by noting that annual U.S. retail sales amount to $2.5 trillion, or nearly one-third of the economy. About $50 billion of that is from catalogue and mail order retailers that rely heavily on UPS.
Wall Street investors got their first taste of the strike's direct impact on Wednesday.

Sport-Haley Inc., a Denver-based sportswear maker, told investors a prolonged stoppage could hurt its earnings by driving up shipping costs. After the announcement, its stock tumbled $2.45 or 15 percent to end at $13.80 on Nasdaq.
UPS, with annual sales of $22.4 billion, also said in a filing with securities regulators that the first national strike in its 90-year history would hurt earnings and probably cost it customers.

Meanwhile, AFL-CIO President John Sweeney said his labour group was ready to help the Teamsters fight an extended battle by providing loans and grants to shore up the union's strike fund, which was to begin disbursing $10 million in weekly strike pay to UPS members next week.
"They haven't made any specific request ... but whatever they need," Sweeney said. "Their struggle is now our struggle."
